facts.statement: More separation from other road users gives you additional time to respond.

evidence.excerpt:
The more distance you keep between yourself and everyone 
else, the more time you have to react.

facts.statement: Following too close can cause a rear-end collision when the leading vehicle stops suddenly.

evidence.excerpt:
They are caused from drivers following too closely to be able to stop 
before hitting the vehicle ahead when it suddenly stops.

facts.statement: For the three-second following check, note when the leading vehicle’s rear passes a fixed roadside marker, then count until you reach that marker.

evidence.excerpt: Watch when the rear of the vehicle ahead passes a sign, pole or any other stationary point.
Count the seconds it takes you to reach the same spot.

facts.statement: If you reach the following-distance marker before completing three seconds, you are too close.

evidence.excerpt: You are following too closely if you pass the mark before you finish counting.
one-thousand-three

facts.statement: Increase the gap and repeat the following-distance check until at least three seconds separate you.

evidence.excerpt:
If so, drop back and then count again at another spot to check the new following distance. Repeat 
until you are following no closer than “three seconds.”

facts.statement: The manual gives a four-second following gap as a potentially needed increase on slippery roads or behind a motorcycle.

evidence.excerpt:
you may need a 
four second following distance to be safe; (1) on slippery roads, (2) when following motorcycles

facts.statement: A heavy load or trailer, or following an emergency vehicle, can require a four-second following gap in the manual’s examples.

evidence.excerpt:
you may need a 
four second following distance to be safe;

(3) 
when you have a heavy load or are pulling a trailer, (4) when following emergency vehicles

facts.statement: The handbook also lists approaching railroad crossings and being stopped on a hill or incline as situations that may need four seconds of following space.

evidence.excerpt:
you may need a 
four second following distance to be safe;

(5) when 
approaching railroad crossings or, (6) when stopped on a hill or incline.

facts.statement: Maintain steady speed and signal slowing or turning early to help a following driver keep a safe gap.

evidence.excerpt:
you can help keep the 
driver at a safe distance by keeping a steady speed and signaling in advance when you have to slow down 
or turn.

facts.statement: Keep space on each side so you have room to turn or change lanes.

evidence.excerpt: You need space on both sides of your vehicle to have room to turn or change lanes.

facts.statement: On a road with at least two lanes, make room for vehicles entering.

evidence.excerpt: Make room for vehicles entering on a roadway that has two or more lanes.

facts.statement: Allow additional side space beside parked cars.

evidence.excerpt: Keep extra space between your vehicle and parked cars.

facts.statement: Give pedestrians and cyclists extra space, with particular care around children.

evidence.excerpt: Give extra space to pedestrians or bicycles, especially children.

facts.statement: The handbook specifies a gap of about four seconds when merging with traffic.

evidence.excerpt: Anytime you want to merge with other traffic, you need a gap of about four seconds.

facts.statement: Entering halfway into a four-second gap leaves roughly two seconds ahead and two seconds behind.

evidence.excerpt:
If you move into the 
middle of a four second gap, both you and the vehicle that is now behind you have a two-second 
following distance.

facts.statement: The handbook applies its four-second merge gap to lane changes, roadway entry and a lane joining another lane.

evidence.excerpt:
You need a four-second gap whenever you change lanes, enter a roadway or when 
your lane merges with another travel lane.

facts.statement: Do not force a merge into insufficient space.

evidence.excerpt: To be safe, do not try to merge into a gap that is too small.

facts.statement: When crossing multiple lanes, move across one lane at a time.

evidence.excerpt: If you want to cross several lanes, take them one at a time.

facts.statement: Crossing traffic requires a gap large enough to clear the entire roadway.

evidence.excerpt: When you cross traffic, you need a large enough gap to get all the way across the road.

facts.statement: Entering traffic requires enough room to complete the turn and accelerate.

evidence.excerpt:
When you enter 
traffic, you need enough space to first turn and then to get up to speed.

facts.statement: Before a left turn, verify that neither vehicles nor pedestrians obstruct your path.

evidence.excerpt: If you are turning left, make sure there are no vehicles or pedestrians blocking your path.

facts.statement: A green signal does not justify starting across when vehicles block your route.

evidence.excerpt:
Even if you have the green light, do not start across the intersection if there are vehicles blocking 
your way.

facts.statement: Enter railroad tracks only with sufficient space to clear them without stopping on the rails.

evidence.excerpt: When you cross railroad tracks, make sure you can cross without having to stop on the tracks.

facts.statement: Even where markings or signs allow passing, independently judge whether enough space makes the maneuver safe.

evidence.excerpt:
Whenever signs or road markings permit you to pass, you will have to judge whether you have enough 
room to pass safely.

facts.statement: As a general practice, overtake one vehicle at a time rather than assuming room to pass several.

evidence.excerpt:
Do not count on having enough time to pass several vehicles at once.  Be safe.  As a 
general rule only pass one vehicle at a time.

facts.statement: At 55 mph, the handbook estimates about ten seconds to pass, requiring corresponding oncoming-traffic and sight-distance gaps.

evidence.excerpt:
At a speed of 55 mph, you need about 10 seconds to pass.  That means you 
need a 10 second gap in oncoming traffic and sight-distance to pass.

facts.statement: For passing near hills and curves, the source requires visibility of at least one-third mile, described as about ten seconds ahead.

evidence.excerpt:
You have to be able to see at least one-third of a mile or about 10 seconds 
ahead.

facts.statement: When a curve or hill blocks the view, assume an approaching vehicle could be hidden beyond it.

evidence.excerpt:
Anytime your view is blocked by a curve or a hill, you should assume that there is an 
oncoming vehicle just out of sight.

facts.statement: Do not begin passing within one-third mile of a hill or curve.

evidence.excerpt:
you should not start to pass if you are within one-third of a mile of 
a hill or curve.

facts.statement: Passing is hazardous at intersections, railroad crossings and shopping entrances where another road user may enter or cross.

evidence.excerpt:
It is dangerous to pass where a vehicle is likely to enter or cross the road.  Such 
places include intersections, railroad crossings and shopping center entrances.

facts.statement: The vehicle being overtaken can hide people, vehicles or trains from your view.

evidence.excerpt:
While you are 
passing, your view of people, vehicles or trains can be blocked by the vehicle you are passing.

facts.statement: Drivers turning right into the lane you use to pass may not expect you there or check your direction.

evidence.excerpt:
drivers turning right into the approaching lane will not expect to find you approaching in 
their lane.  They may not even look your way before turning.

facts.statement: Before overtaking, scan for conditions that may push other road users into your intended lane.

evidence.excerpt:
Before you pass, look ahead for road conditions and traffic that may cause 
other vehicles to move into your lane.

facts.statement: Pedestrians or cyclists near the roadway can reduce the space available for passing.

evidence.excerpt:
Due to lane restrictions, you might lose your space and it 
may not be safe to pass:
people or bicyclists near the road

facts.statement: A narrow bridge, reduced lane width, ice, potholes or roadway debris can remove passing room.

evidence.excerpt: a narrow bridge or other situation that causes reduced lane width, or
a patch of ice, pothole or something on the road.

facts.statement: Pass only when room exists to return to the driving lane; do not rely on others to create that room.

evidence.excerpt:
Do not pass unless you have enough space to return to the driving lane. Do not 
count on other drivers to make room for you.

facts.statement: Do not overtake with a railroad grade crossing ahead.

evidence.excerpt: Do not pass if there is a railroad grade crossing ahead.

facts.statement: Before returning after passing, leave enough clearance; the manual’s visual cue is seeing both headlights of the passed vehicle in the rearview mirror.

evidence.excerpt:
Before you return to the driving lane, be sure to leave enough room between yourself and the vehicle you 
have passed.  When you can see both headlights of the vehicle you just passed in your rear-view mirror, it 
is safe to return to the driving lane.

facts.statement: On roads, bicycle operators have the rights and responsibilities of car drivers.

evidence.excerpt: Bicycle drivers on roads  have the same rights and responsibilities

as drivers 
of cars.

facts.statement: When overtaking a cyclist, keep safe clearance, aim for at least five feet, and pass only where safe and legal.

evidence.excerpt: Keep a safe distance when passing a bicyclist, trying for at least
five feet
and passing them only when safe and legal to do so.

facts.statement: Allow cyclists additional space and time to merge or use a turn lane.

evidence.excerpt:
Provide the bicyclist with extra time and space to merge and use 
turn lanes like other vehicles.

facts.statement: Treat a bicycle as a lawful slow vehicle, as you would a backhoe.

evidence.excerpt: Treat the bicycle as a legal, slow-moving vehicle such as a backhoe.

facts.statement: Although cyclists usually stay right, they may lawfully use the lane’s center and occupy the entire lane when necessary.

evidence.excerpt:
While bicycles should usually stay on the right side of the roadway, they are legally allowed to 
take the whole lane by riding in the center of the traffic lane when necessary.

facts.statement: Typical reasons for a cyclist to occupy the full lane include preparing to turn left, avoiding a squeeze on a narrow street, or avoiding grates, debris and other hazards.

evidence.excerpt:
typically take the whole lane to prepare for a left turn, to avoid 
being squeezed on a narrow street, or to avoid hazards, grates and 
debris,
Bicyclists will

facts.statement: With a cyclist on your right, avoid passing then making a sudden right turn; slow and merge behind the cyclist before turning.

evidence.excerpt:
Do  not  make  a  sudden  right  turn  after  passing  a  bicyclist  on  
your  right. Instead, slow down and merge behind the bicyclist 
before turning.

facts.statement: Expect unexpected movement or lane changes from some cyclists, particularly young children.

evidence.excerpt:
Some bicyclists, especially young children, will behave 
unexpectedly. Stay watchful for sudden movements and lane 
changes.

facts.statement: Cyclists must follow traffic signals, signs and laws as car drivers do.

evidence.excerpt: Obey all traffic signals, laws and signs, just as if driving a car

facts.statement: The bicycle requirements described by the handbook include a bright front light and effective rear reflector at night.

evidence.excerpt:
including night-time use of a bright headlight and good, rear 
reflector.

facts.statement: Cyclists must ride with traffic and make turns in the same manner as cars.

evidence.excerpt:
Travel in the same direction as traffic, making left and right turns 
in the same way cars do.

facts.statement: The handbook requires cyclists to signal turns and stops by hand, with the gestures shown in its illustrations.

evidence.excerpt: Use these hand signals to indicate turning and stopping.

facts.statement: Cyclists can improve conspicuity through bright clothing, suitable lighting and predictable movement.

evidence.excerpt:
Bicycles may be difficult for motorists to see. Wear bright colors, 
use proper lighting, and be predictable.

facts.statement: The source describes riding with the ordinary flow of traffic as the safest bicycle position in traffic.

evidence.excerpt:
The safest way to ride is as part of the traffic, going with the flow 
of the normal traffic pattern.

facts.statement: The manual advises well-fitting helmets for adults and states that minors must wear them.

evidence.excerpt: Adults should, and minors must, wear a well-fitting helmet.

facts.statement: Sharrows are pavement symbols marking shared travel lanes.

evidence.excerpt: “Sharrows” are “shared lane pavement markings.”

facts.statement: The handbook places sharrows where a road is too narrow for side-by-side sharing with slower vehicles.

evidence.excerpt:
They are 
painted on the pavement when a road is too narrow for side-by-
side road sharing with slower vehicles.

facts.statement: A sharrow encourages cyclists to use the full lane and requires motorists to yield when needed.

evidence.excerpt:
They indicate that 
bicyclists are encouraged to take the whole travel lane and that 
motorists shall yield to the bicyclist as needed.

facts.statement: At sharrows, motorists should reduce speed and yield to cyclists occupying the roadway.

evidence.excerpt: Slow down and yield to bicyclists in the roadway.

facts.statement: At sharrows, pass a cyclist only when roadway width permits the cyclist to move right.

evidence.excerpt:
Pass bicyclists only when the roadway width allows bicyclists 
to move to the right.

facts.statement: The sharrow guidance asks motorists to try for at least five feet of passing clearance.

evidence.excerpt:
Try to give bicyclists at least five feet of clearance when 
passing.

facts.statement: A cyclist may ride down the sharrow’s center.

evidence.excerpt: As a bicyclist, you may ride on the center of the sharrow.

facts.statement: Cyclists should keep clear of the area where a parked car’s door may open.

evidence.excerpt: Keep a safe distance from the “door zone” of parked cars.

facts.statement: Cyclists should move right to allow a vehicle past when doing so is safe.

evidence.excerpt: Move right to let vehicles pass when it is safe to do so.

facts.statement: A large truck or RV requires more stopping distance than a car at the same speed.

evidence.excerpt: Large trucks and RVs take longer to stop than a car going the same speed.

facts.statement: In the manual’s 55-mph comparison, an average car stops in about 400 feet while a large truck may need almost 800 feet.

evidence.excerpt:
Large trucks and RVs take longer to stop than a car going the same speed. An average car 
going 55 mph can stop in about 400 feet. But a large truck could take almost 800 feet to stop.

facts.statement: Do not pull ahead of a big truck and abruptly slow or stop; it may be unable to stop before striking you.

evidence.excerpt:
don’t 
pull in front of a big rig and suddenly slow down or stop. The driver may not be able to stop quickly 
enough to avoid crashing into you.

facts.statement: Trucks and RVs need extra turning room and may swing wide for a right turn.

evidence.excerpt:
Big trucks and RVs need more room to make turns. They often swing wide to make a right 
turn.

facts.statement: Before passing a large vehicle you are following, inspect its turn signals.

evidence.excerpt: When you follow a big rig, look at its turn signals before you start to pass.

facts.statement: If a truck appears to turn left, pause and recheck its signals because it may actually be setting up a right turn.

evidence.excerpt:
If you think the truck is 
turning left, wait a second and check the turn signals again. The driver may really be turning right.

facts.statement: A truck’s elevated seat and large mirrors do not eliminate its broad blind areas, called the NO ZONE.

evidence.excerpt:
they can see 
better in front of them and they have bigger mirrors. But there are still large areas they can’t see. These 
are called their “blind spots” or the “NO ZONE.”

facts.statement: Stay out of truck blind spots; an unseen vehicle could be struck if the truck swerves around a hazard.

evidence.excerpt:
Don’t drive in a trucker’s blind spots. You might be in 
the way if the trucker swerves to avoid a hazard.

facts.statement: As a general cue, if the truck’s driver is invisible to you in its side mirror, the driver cannot see you.

evidence.excerpt:
In general, if you can’t see the driver in the side mirror, 
the driver can’t see you.

facts.statement: Do not cut into a truck’s or RV’s forward space to reach an exit or turn.

evidence.excerpt:
Don’t cut in front of a truck or RV in traffic to reach your exit or turn. Cutting into the open space 
in front of a truck is dangerous.

facts.statement: Avoid driving alongside a truck or RV because it may need that space to avoid a road hazard.

evidence.excerpt:
Don’t drive beside a large truck or RV. If you drive beside the truck or RV, they may not be able 
to swerve to miss a hazard in the road.

facts.statement: The handbook directs passing trucks and RVs on their left, then moving ahead rather than lingering in a blind spot.

evidence.excerpt:
Always pass a large truck or RV on the left side. After you pass, move ahead of it. Don’t stay in 
the driver’s blind spot.

facts.statement: Do not tailgate a truck; its driver may not know you are close behind.

evidence.excerpt:
Don’t follow too closely or tailgate. If you drive too close behind a truck, the trucker may not know you 
are there.

facts.statement: A large truck or RV may appear to be traveling slower than its actual speed.

evidence.excerpt: Remember that a big truck or RV may look like it’s going more slowly than it is.
